<!-- Source: website/content/docs/concepts/lifecycle.mdx -->

---
title: Lifecycle
description: How sessions are created, ended and torn down on both runtimes, and what is cleaned up in 1.1.0.
---

## WebXR path

### Create

`ARView.create()` calls `engine.startSession()`. Three.js objects are
created **once**, the first start builds the renderer, scene, camera,
lights, loader, plane groups and reticle, and are reused across
sessions. The renderer canvas is inserted before your overlay element
(or appended to `document.body` when there is no overlay).

### Session end (user or system)

When the XR session ends on its own (user exits, system interrupts):

- the engine fires `sessionEnded` to frame listeners,
- the animation loop stops,
- session / hit-test-source / reference-space fields are nulled,

…but placed models and the canvas are **not** removed. That only happens
in `stopSession()`. Listen for `sessionEnded` and call
`ar.destroy()` (or start again, like the demo's Resume flow) to return
to a clean state.

### Teardown

`ARView.destroy()` destroys the gesture controller and awaits
`engine.dispose()`, the full teardown (in 1.0.0 destroy only stopped
the session; the rest of this list is 1.1.0 behaviour). Disposal:

- stops rendering and ends the XR session,
- removes models, shadow planes and base rings from the scene and
  clears the anchor/model maps, disposing per-instance GPU
  resources (removed/switched models are disposed on those paths
  too, under the engine's ownership rule),
- disposes plane dots and meshes,
- hides the reticle and removes the canvas from the DOM,
- disposes the model cache, the WebGL renderer and its context,
  and nulls the renderer/scene/camera fields, the same engine
  instance can be started again afterwards.

### React

- `ARPlayground`-style components: construct one `ARView` per mount,
  `destroy()` in the effect cleanup.
- `useARCore`: checks support on mount; on unmount it stops the session
  if it started one and runs its listener cleanups. By default all
  consumers share one lazily-constructed engine, so that stop affects
  **all** hook consumers; mount the hook once, or pass a dedicated
  engine per view with `useARCore({ engine })`.

## Native path

### Create

The plugin's `load()` constructs its managers once; the Filament
engine is created **lazily** on first use (if it cannot initialise,
session entry points fail with a coded `FILAMENT_UNAVAILABLE`
instead of leaving the renderer in a broken state).
`startSession` then: camera permission → ARCore availability / install →
`Session` creation and configuration → native view inserted behind the
WebView, which is made transparent.

### Pause and resume

Wired in 1.1.0 (in v1.0.0 nothing called the pause/resume methods,
the gap this section used to describe). The plugin implements
Capacitor's `handleOnPause` / `handleOnResume` / `handleOnDestroy`
and forwards them to the session manager and renderer:

- Backgrounding the activity pauses the ARCore session and the
  render loop, as ARCore's contract requires.
- A dedicated stop flag (not the pause flag) tracks `stopSession`,
  so a session restarted after a stop in the same app run renders
  normally.

### Teardown

`stopSession` (on the UI thread): clears models/anchors → renderer
session-closed → view removed and the WebView's real background
restored → session closed. Plugin destroy goes further: it stops
the render loop, **joins the render thread**, then destroys the
Filament resources in dependency order, camera background, swap
chain, view, scene, renderer, camera entity, and the engine last.


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/concepts/webxr-vs-native.mdx -->

---
title: WebXR vs native ARCore
description: "An honest feature-by-feature split of the package's two runtimes in 1.1.0: what each one actually does, verified against the code."
---

The package contains two AR runtimes that share a JS facade name and
almost nothing else. Earlier README wording presented them as "two
runtimes, one API" at feature parity. They are not. This page is the
corrected, code-verified split, updated for 1.1.0.

## Feature by feature

| Capability | WebXR runtime (`src/web.js`) | Native Android (`android/`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Session start/stop | Yes, `immersive-ar` XR session | Yes, ARCore `Session` via the plugin |
| Plane detection | Yes, XR planes, dot/mesh visualisation | Yes, planes tracked, surface state events |
| Hit testing | Yes, centre reticle path; non-centre coordinates use a ray-based hit test | Yes, real per-coordinate hit test against the frame, served by the render loop |
| **Model rendering** | **Yes, GLB/GLTF via Three.js, anchored in the scene** | **No, `placeModel` rejects with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`; there is no native renderer (Option B, see below)** |
| Model transforms | Yes, position/rotation/scale on placed models | `setTransform` / `setMaterial` reject with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` |
| `moveModel` | Hit-test based (centre or ray) | Rejects with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` |
| Colours / textures | Yes, materials are real and rendered | Via the WebXR runtime only |
| Anchors | Yes, XR anchors drive model poses per frame | Hit tests create real ARCore anchors and return their `anchorId`; there are no native model placements to anchor |
| Screenshots | Yes, camera + scene composite (needs the `enableScreenshots` opt-in) | No |
| Gestures | Yes, Pointer Events controller over the DOM overlay | Via your web UI (the WebView stays on top) |
| Support check | Real, feature detection against `navigator.xr`, with an `INSECURE_CONTEXT` code outside secure contexts | Real, `ArCoreApk.checkAvailability()`; unsupported devices and missing ARCore are reported honestly |
| Pause/resume with the activity | Browser-managed | Wired, the plugin forwards Capacitor's pause/resume/destroy to the session and render loop |

## Which runtime am I on?

- `createARView`, the functional helpers and `useARCore` → **always
  WebXR**, in a browser and inside a Capacitor app alike.
- The `ARCore` facade → native plugin on Android; on web platforms the
  same plugin name resolves to the WebXR engine, so facade calls in a
  browser behave like the engine (including rendering).

## Guidance

- **Building a product viewer today:** use the WebXR path
  (`createARView`). It is the only runtime that renders models, and it
  runs on ARCore-capable Android devices through Chrome or the Capacitor
  WebView.
- **Planning on the native path:** it is **session + hit-test +
  surface events**, by decision (audit Option B): the model methods
  reject with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` rather than reporting success for
  work that never happened. Native model rendering (Option A) remains
  an owner decision, not a roadmap promise.
- **Support gating:** either runtime's `checkSupport()` is a real
  check in 1.1.0: the WebXR one feature-detects `navigator.xr` (and
  reports `INSECURE_CONTEXT` outside secure contexts), the native one
  asks ARCore itself. Still handle `startSession` failure: support
  can change between the check and the session (installs, updates,
  permissions).

<Note>
None of this makes the native layer useless: availability handling,
install flow, session configuration, plane tracking, real hit-test
anchors and the render loop for the camera background are real,
working code. The gap is specific, model rendering, and it is
documented here rather than discovered by users.
</Note>


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/colors-and-textures.mdx -->

---
title: Colors & textures
description: Recolour the placed model, register and apply your own textures, and tune material properties, plus the multi-material caveats.
---

## Recolouring the active model

```js
await ar.placeModel('/models/sofa.glb');
await ar.setColor('#68705b'); // hex string, applied to the active model
```

`ARView.setColor(color)` applies to the active model only. It is the
building block for the colour swatches in the [live demo](/demo) and the
example app:

```jsx title="Swatches.jsx"
const SWATCHES = [
  ['Beige', '#c8b49b'],
  ['Grey', '#858585'],
  ['Olive', '#68705b'],
  ['Navy', '#222b3c'],
  ['Terracotta', '#a55f3b'],
];

{SWATCHES.map(([name, hex]) => (
  <button key={hex} data-ui onClick={() => ar.setColor(hex)}>
    {name}
  </button>
))}
```

## Textures

Register named texture URLs once, then apply them by name (or pass a URL
directly). `addTextures` returns the view, so calls chain:

```js
ar.addTextures({
  oak: '/textures/oak.jpg',
  walnut: '/textures/walnut.jpg',
});

await ar.applyTexture('oak');                       // by registered name
await ar.applyTexture('/textures/marble.jpg');      // or by URL
await ar.applyTexture('oak', { materialName: 'Top' }); // one named material only
```

- `applyTexture` **throws if no model is placed**, call it after a
  successful `placeModel`/`switchModel`.
- `materialName` targets a single material inside the GLB; without it the
  texture applies across the model's materials.
- Texture URLs follow the same rules as model URLs: app-controlled,
  CORS-enabled if cross-origin.

<Note>
Two engine-level behaviours to design around:

- Applying a texture replaces the previous one on the material; since
  1.1.0 the replaced texture is disposed (unless it is the model's
  original, cache-owned map), so flipping through dozens of swatches in
  one session no longer leaks a GPU texture per application. (v1.0.0
  leaked one texture per application, see
  [known issues](/docs/known-issues).)
- When `switchModel` carries material state over (`preserveMaterial`, the
  default), materials are matched by name, then by traversal order, so
  multi-material products keep their per-material styling, see
  [Model preloading & switching](/docs/guides/model-preloading-and-switching#material-carry-over).
</Note>

## Material properties (engine / hook level)

The facade exposes colour and texture. Finer material control lives one
layer down, on the engine, and through the hook:

```js
// Via useARCore():
ar.setModelMaterial(modelId, { metalness: 0.1, roughness: 0.8, opacity: 1 });
```

`setModelMaterial({ modelId, metalness?, roughness?, opacity? })` sets
the given PBR properties on the anchored model's materials. All three
properties are optional; omitted ones are left unchanged. There is no
facade (`ARView`) wrapper for this, if you hold an `ARView`,
its engine is `ar.engine` and accepts the same call with an options
object.

## Native facade equivalent

The native `ARCore` facade exposes `setMaterial({ modelId, color })`
with the same `modelId` convention (the engine's old name, `anchorId`,
still works as a deprecated alias), but on Android the call rejects
with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`: colour and material changes are
WebXR-runtime features. See the
[API reference](/docs/api#arcore-native-facade).


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/gestures.mdx -->

---
title: Gestures
description: Tap to place, drag, pinch to scale and two-finger twist to rotate, via ARView.enableCustomization or the standalone gesture controller.
---

## The built-in wiring: `enableCustomization`

The fastest way to get gestures is `ARView.enableCustomization()`. It
attaches a gesture controller to the view's overlay and wires the gestures
to the active model:

```js title="gestures.js"
const cleanup = ar.enableCustomization({
  // REQUIRED: which model a tap should place. A plain URL string works;
  // pass a function and it is called on every tap, so the model placed
  // can follow the user's current selection.
  modelUrl: () => currentModelUrl,
  onTap: () => console.log('placed'),
  onScale: (factor) => console.log('scale is now', factor),
  onRotate: (radians) => console.log('rotationY is now', radians),
});

// Later, to detach:
cleanup();
```

| Gesture | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| One-finger tap | Places the current `modelUrl` at the tap point; with a model already placed, moves it to the tap point |
| Pinch (two fingers, in/out) | Scales the active model, `ARView.setScale` clamps to **[0.1, 5]** |
| Twist (two fingers, rotate) | Rotates the active model around Y |
| Drag (one finger) | Drags the active model across surfaces: the engine re-aims a hit test at your finger every frame, so the model stays under it, and one final move lands it exactly on the release point. Passing over a spot with no surface is silent; the model stays at its last good position |

<Note>
`modelUrl` accepts a plain URL string or a `() => string` function.
The function form is called on every tap; use it when the model to
place can change between taps (the example app reads the latest
selected product from a ref). A plain string always places the same
model. (Before 1.1.0 only the function form worked; a string threw a
`TypeError` inside the tap handler.)
</Note>

Overlay elements marked with `data-ui` are ignored by the gesture layer,
so your buttons and sheets never double as scene gestures.

## The standalone controller

For custom interactions, use the exported controller directly. It is
framework-agnostic Pointer Events code and knows nothing about AR:

```js title="custom-gestures.js"
import { createARGestureController } from 'reticlexr';

const gestures = createARGestureController({
  element: document.querySelector('#ar-overlay'), // required
  onTap: ({ x, y }) => { /* pointerup point, px */ },
  onDrag: ({ dx, dy, x, y }) => { /* per-move deltas, px */ },
  onPinch: ({ factor, center }) => { /* factor is incremental */ },
  onRotate: ({ delta, center }) => { /* delta in radians, incremental */ },
  tapMaxDuration: 260,   // ms: longer presses are not taps
  tapMaxDistance: 12,    // px: further movement is not a tap
  preventDefault: true,
  ignoreSelector: '[data-ui]',
});

// When the view goes away:
gestures.destroy();
```

Payload semantics worth knowing:

- `onPinch`'s `factor` is **incremental**, relative to the previous move
  event, not the gesture start. Multiply your running scale by it.
- `onRotate`'s `delta` is likewise incremental, in radians, wrapped to
  ±π.
- A tap is a pointer down/up pair within `tapMaxDuration` and
  `tapMaxDistance`. One known quirk: a `pointercancel` (system
  gesture, notification) that happens to be short and stationary is
  currently treated as a completed tap and can place a model.

## Driving transforms yourself

If you bypass `enableCustomization`, the facade exposes the same
operations the gestures use:

```js
ar.setScale(1.4);        // clamped to [0.1, 5], applied uniformly
ar.rotateBy(Math.PI / 8); // accumulates rotationY, radians
```

One scale range everywhere since 1.1.0: [0.1, 5], enforced by the
engine itself (the facade and the native registry use the same
limits). In v1.0.0 the layers disagreed: facade [0.1, 5], engine
unclamped, native [0.25, 3].


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/model-preloading-and-switching.mdx -->

---
title: Model preloading & switching
description: How the model cache works, why preloadModels makes switching fast, and why switchModel, never placeModel, is the switching call.
---

## Preloading

`preloadModels(urls)` loads each URL through the engine's GLTF loader and
stores the parsed result in the engine's model cache:

```js
await ar.preloadModels(['/models/sofa.glb', '/models/chair.glb', '/models/table.glb']);
```

Every later placement of a cached URL clones from the parsed in-memory
model instead of fetching and parsing again. For a product catalogue,
preload the visible products when the AR view is created (or when the
product page loads), so the first tap doesn't pay network + parse time.

Things to know about the cache:

- It is keyed by URL. The cache is LRU-capped
  (`config.modelCacheLimit`, default 20); entries with live
  placements are never evicted, and the engine's
  `clearModelCache()` empties it explicitly. (In v1.0.0 there was
  no eviction, every URL you loaded stayed resident.)
- Preloading is a `Promise.all` over the URLs: one failing URL rejects
  the batch. Load stragglers individually if your catalogue has optional
  items.
- Model files are fetched with the page's origin rules, cross-origin
  models need CORS headers from the host serving them, and URLs must be
  app-controlled (the loader parses whatever it is given).

## Switching models in place

Use `switchModel()` to change the product a shopper is looking at:

```js
// The shopper placed the sofa and scaled it to fit the corner.
await ar.switchModel('/models/chair.glb');
// The chair appears at the same anchor, with the same scale and rotation.
```

`switchModel(modelUrl, { preserveMaterial = true })`:

- Keeps the existing anchor, position, scale and rotation.
- With `preserveMaterial` (the default), carries the current colour/texture
  over to the new model.
- Falls back to a fresh `placeModel()` when nothing is placed yet, so it
  is safe to call from a product-switcher UI unconditionally.

<Warning>
**Do not use `placeModel()` to switch.** `placeModel` always performs a
fresh hit test and creates a *new* model alongside the previous one,
the placement, scale and rotation you had do not carry over. (Both
models stay tracked: `getPlacedModels()` lists them and
`clearModels()` removes them.) An earlier version of the README's API
table (and its React example) claimed `placeModel` switching "keeps
placement, scale and rotation"; that was wrong, and the docs now teach
`switchModel`.
</Warning>

## Removing the model

```js
await ar.removeModel(); // removes the active model; no-op if none is placed
```

`ARView` tracks every model placed through it, with a single **active
model**. `removeModel()` removes the active one and clears the active
id/URL. `getPlacedModels()` enumerates everything placed through the
view and `clearModels()` removes all of it, but switching with
`switchModel()` is still the right tool for product changes: it reuses
the placement instead of stacking models.

## Material carry-over

With `preserveMaterial`, each material of the new model inherits the
colour, and the map, when present, from its counterpart on the old
model, matched **by material name first, then by traversal order**
(fixed in 1.1.0; before that, the first material was copied
onto every material). Materials without a counterpart keep their own
look. If you prefer explicit styling, pass
`{ preserveMaterial: false }` and re-apply with
[`setColor`](/docs/guides/colors-and-textures) /
`applyTexture` after the switch.


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/overlays.mdx -->

---
title: Overlays
description: "Your product UI as regular DOM on top of the immersive view: how the overlay element works and how data-ui keeps buttons out of the gesture layer."
---

## The overlay element

An `ARView` is bound to one DOM element, the **overlay**. You pass it to
the constructor (or later to `create()`):

```js
const ar = createARView({ overlay: document.querySelector('#ar-overlay') });
await ar.create({ /* … */ });
```

When the session starts, that element is handed to the browser as the XR
session's DOM overlay: it stays visible and interactive on top of the
camera view while the session is immersive. Everything inside it is
ordinary DOM, your product cards, price tags, variant pickers and
checkout buttons, styled however you like.

```html title="overlay.html"
<div id="ar-overlay">
  <header data-ui>
    <button id="close-ar">×</button>
    <span>AR View</span>
  </header>

  <div class="product-card" data-ui>
    <strong>Sofa — $899</strong>
    <button id="add-to-cart">Add to cart</button>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Keeping UI out of the gesture layer

The gesture controller ignores pointer events that land on elements
matching `[data-ui]` (the `ignoreSelector` default). Mark every
interactive overlay element, or a wrapper around them, with `data-ui`:

- Buttons, links, inputs, sheets and dialogs: **mark them.**
- Empty areas of the overlay: leave unmarked, so taps, pinches and
  twists reach the scene.

In React, the attribute is just `data-ui` (any value, including none):

```jsx
<button data-ui onClick={addToCart}>Add to cart</button>
```

The repository's example and this site's [demo](/demo) both follow this
pattern: header, product strip, swatch sheet and dialogs are `data-ui`;
the rest of the overlay surface drives gestures.

## Without an overlay

`createARView()` can be constructed without an overlay. The session then
runs without a DOM overlay (the renderer canvas is appended to
`document.body`), and `enableCustomization()`, which needs an element
to listen on, throws. If you want gestures, you need an overlay; if you
only place models programmatically, you don't.

## The native path is different

In a Capacitor Android app, there is no WebXR DOM overlay: the plugin
inserts a native AR view *behind* the WebView and makes the WebView
transparent during a session, so your web UI visually floats over the
native camera view. The programming model (your DOM stays your DOM) is
the same; the mechanism is not.


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/react-integration.mdx -->

---
title: React integration
description: "Two ways to use the SDK from React: an ARView held in a ref for product viewers, and the useARCore hook when you want engine state in React state."
---

There are two React-shaped ways to use the SDK. Pick based on how much of
the engine you want mirrored into React state:

- **`createARView()` in a ref**, the pattern the repository's example uses.
  Best for product viewers: the engine runs imperatively, React only tracks
  UI state (active product, placed or not, current scale).
- **[`useARCore()`](/docs/api#usearcore)**, a hook that wraps the engine
  and mirrors support, session, placed models, planes, surface state and
  errors into React state.

## Product viewer with `createARView`

```jsx title="ProductAR.jsx"
import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { createARView } from 'reticlexr';

const MODELS = {
  Sofa: '/models/sofa.glb',
  Chair: '/models/chair.glb',
};

export default function ProductAR() {
  const overlayRef = useRef(null);
  const arRef = useRef(null);
  const [active, setActive] = useState('Sofa');

  useEffect(() => {
    const ar = createARView({ overlay: overlayRef.current });
    arRef.current = ar;
    return () => {
      ar.destroy().catch(() => {});
      arRef.current = null;
    };
  }, []);

  async function start() {
    const ar = arRef.current;
    await ar.create({ showReticle: true, showPlaneDots: true });
    await ar.preloadModels(Object.values(MODELS));
    await ar.placeModel(MODELS[active]);
  }

  async function switchTo(name) {
    setActive(name);
    // switchModel, NOT placeModel, keeps placement, scale and rotation.
    await arRef.current?.switchModel(MODELS[name]);
  }

  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={start}>View in your room</button>
      <div id="ar-overlay" ref={overlayRef}>
        {Object.keys(MODELS).map((name) => (
          <button key={name} data-ui onClick={() => switchTo(name)}>
            {name}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
    </>
  );
}
```

Three details matter:

1. **One `ARView` per mount, destroyed in the cleanup.** `destroy()` ends
   the XR session and removes the placed models. Under React StrictMode's
   dev double-mount you will build a throwaway engine instance, harmless
   in production, noticeable as extra startup cost in dev.
2. **`data-ui` on interactive overlay children.** The gesture layer
   ignores pointer events on elements matching `[data-ui]`, so buttons
   don't also place or drag the model.
3. **`switchModel` for switching.** The older README example used
   `placeModel` here with a comment claiming state carries over; it does
   not. `placeModel` performs a fresh centre hit test and adds a new model
   (the old one stays placed: list them with `getPlacedModels()`, remove
   them with `clearModels()`). See
   [Model preloading & switching](/docs/guides/model-preloading-and-switching).

## The `useARCore` hook

```jsx title="HookExample.jsx"
import { useARCore } from 'reticlexr/react';

export default function HookExample({ overlayRef }) {
  const ar = useARCore();

  if (ar.isSupported === null) return <p>Checking AR support…</p>;
  if (ar.isSupported === false) return <p>AR is not available here.</p>;

  return (
    <div>
      <button
        onClick={() => ar.startSession({ domOverlay: overlayRef.current })}
        disabled={ar.isSessionActive}
      >
        Start AR
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => ar.placeModel('/models/sofa.glb')}>
        Place sofa
      </button>
      <p>
        Planes: {ar.detectedPlanes.total} · Surface:{' '}
        {ar.surfaceState.hasSurface ? ar.surfaceState.planeType : 'none'}
      </p>
      {ar.error && <p role="alert">{ar.error}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

The hook returns state (`isSupported`, `isSessionActive`, `placedModels`,
`detectedPlanes`, `surfaceState`, `error`) and methods mirroring the
engine; the full list is in the [API reference](/docs/api#usearcore).

<Warning>
Two hook facts to design around:

- **Shared engine by default.** All `useARCore()` consumers share one
  lazily-constructed engine instance. When any one consumer unmounts,
  its cleanup stops the session for all of them. Mount the hook in
  exactly one place in your tree (or lift it into a provider you
  control), or pass a dedicated engine per view:
  `useARCore({ engine })` with a `new ARCoreWeb()` from
  `reticlexr/web`.
- **Transform argument shapes are normalised.** The hook's
  `placeModel(modelUrl, position, rotation, scale)` accepts arrays
  (`[x, y, z]`, quaternion `[x, y, z, w]`, `[sx, sy, sz]`) **or**
  `{x, y, z}` objects, and Euler-radian rotations; scales clamp to
  [0.1, 5]. (In v1.0.0, objects produced `NaN` transforms, fixed
  in 1.1.0.)
</Warning>

## Overlays and SSR

Overlay children are regular React DOM rendered into the element you pass
as `overlay`; the same element is handed to the XR session as its
DOM overlay. Styling, routing and state inside it are entirely yours,
see [Overlays](/docs/guides/overlays).

<Todo>
SSR: import-time side effects were removed in 1.1.0 (the event
bridge installs lazily on first subscription; the shared hook
engine is constructed lazily), and all five entry points pass
DOM-less import checks, importing them touches no
`window`/`document`, and the hook renders to string. A full
framework prerender (e.g. Next.js) has **not** been exercised yet,
so that remains TODO: until it is verified, loading AR components
client-side only (e.g. Next.js `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })`) is
the safe default, which is what this site's own [demo](/demo)
does.
</Todo>


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/screenshots.mdx -->

---
title: Screenshots
description: "Capture the composited AR view to a data URL: what the result contains, and why it can return CAMERA_CAPTURE_UNAVAILABLE."
---

## Taking a screenshot

Screenshots that include the camera feed need the session started
with the screenshot opt-in (see the warning below):

```js
await ar.create({ enableScreenshots: true }); // ARView
// or, on the engine/hook: startSession({ enableScreenshots: true })

const shot = await ar.takeScreenshot({ format: 'png', includeReticle: false });

if (shot.success) {
  // shot.dataUrl: 'data:image/png;base64,…'
  // shot.width / shot.height
  // shot.timestamp
  // shot.includesCamera: whether the camera feed is in the image
  const img = new Image();
  img.src = shot.dataUrl;
  document.body.appendChild(img);
} else {
  console.warn(shot.code, shot.error);
}
```

Options (all optional):

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `format` | `'png'` | `'png'` or `'jpeg'` |
| `quality` | `0.92` | JPEG quality (ignored for PNG) |
| `width` / `height` | canvas size | Output dimensions |
| `includeReticle` | engine default | Whether the placement reticle is composited in |

The same call exists as a functional helper,
`takeScreenshot(view, options)`, and on the `useARCore` hook.

## Saving the image

A data URL is all you get back, turning it into a download or an upload
is your app's job:

```js title="save-shot.js"
function downloadShot(shot) {
  const a = document.createElement('a');
  a.href = shot.dataUrl;
  a.download = `ar-${shot.timestamp}.png`;
  a.click();
}
```

## When screenshots fail

Screenshots composite the **camera image** with the rendered scene, which
needs the WebXR `camera-access` feature. Two failure codes exist:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `CAMERA_CAPTURE_UNAVAILABLE` | The browser/session has no camera access; the capture cannot include the camera feed |
| `CAPTURE_BUSY` | Another capture is already in flight |

<Warning>
Camera access is an explicit opt-in: the session must start with
`enableScreenshots: true` (`ARView.create()` or the engine's
`startSession()`), which adds `camera-access` to the session's
optional features. It is **not** implied by `lightEstimation`
(that coupling was removed in 1.1.0). Without the opt-in,
or on browsers that don't grant camera access at all,
`takeScreenshot` returns `CAMERA_CAPTURE_UNAVAILABLE` while AR
keeps running. Design your UI to treat screenshots as best-effort,
and always branch on `shot.success`.
</Warning>

<Note>
Composition runs as a per-pixel loop on the main thread (~2M iterations
at 1080p), so expect a visible hitch on capture. Fine for a shutter
button; don't call it per frame.
</Note>


---

<!-- Source: website/content/docs/guides/troubleshooting.mdx -->

---
title: Troubleshooting
description: "Symptom-by-symptom fixes: several entries describe v1.0.0 behaviours that 1.1.0 fixed; each says which."
---

## AR won't start on my phone, but works on desktop localhost

Almost certainly the **secure context**. WebXR immersive AR requires
HTTPS (or `localhost`). A LAN address over plain HTTP loads the page
but session creation fails; `checkSupport()` reports
`{ supported: false, code: 'INSECURE_CONTEXT' }` so you can tell this
case apart from a genuinely unsupported device. Serve the page over
HTTPS, see
[HTTPS and phone testing](/docs/getting-started#https-and-phone-testing),
or open this site's [live demo](/demo), which is already HTTPS.

## The session fails immediately on some Android devices

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** Session creation used to hard-require
the WebXR `local-floor` feature; devices with immersive AR + hit-test
but no `local-floor` failed outright. The engine now requests
`local-floor` first and falls back to `local`, then `viewer`. If a
session still fails immediately, check the secure context (above)
and that the `hit-test` feature is available, that one is still
required.

## `checkSupport()` says yes, but the native session fails later

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The native facade's `checkSupport` used
to resolve `{supported: true}` unconditionally. It now returns the
real `ArCoreApk.checkAvailability()` result, so an unsupported or
ARCore-less device reports `supported: false` up front. Still handle
`startSession` failure: availability can change between the check
and the session (installs, updates, permissions).

## My model never appears (hook `placeModel`)

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The hook's `placeModel(modelUrl,
position, rotation, scale)` used to require array shapes while its
JSDoc described `{x, y, z}` objects, objects produced `NaN`
transforms and invisible models. Transform inputs are now normalised
at the engine boundary: positions accept `[x, y, z]` **or**
`{x, y, z}`, rotations a quaternion array/object or Euler radians,
scales a number, array or object (clamped to [0.1, 5]). If a model
still never appears, check the `placeModel` result for an `error` /
`code` (e.g. `NO_SURFACE`, no surface was hit yet).

## `detectedPlanes` in the hook is always zero

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The hook read array fields while the
engine emits plane counts as numbers; it now reads the numbers.
Plane listeners (`ARView.onPlanes()`, the engine's plane listener)
receive `{type, total, horizontal, vertical}` as before.

## `placeModel(url, {x, y})` ignores where I tapped

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The WebXR `hitTest({x, y})` used to
ignore its coordinates and always return the centre-screen hit.
Non-centre coordinates now perform a ray-based hit test
(`hitTestAtPoint`), so tap-point placement works; the centre
coordinates still use the reticle path.

## My reticle setting keeps turning back on

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** `showReticle: false` used to be forced
back to `true` on session start, placement and removal. The setting
is now honoured; `setReticleVisible(false)` also persists.

## Every tap throws `TypeError: options.modelUrl is not a function`

Older versions required `enableCustomization({ modelUrl })` to be a
**function**. In 1.1.0 it accepts a URL string **or** a
`() => string` function (use the function when the current product
can change between taps). If you still see this error, you're on a
pre-1.1.0 build. See [Gestures](/docs/guides/gestures).

## Memory grows while users browse products

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** Removed/switched models are now
disposed under a documented ownership rule, plane dots are disposed
with their planes, and the model cache is LRU-capped
(`config.modelCacheLimit`, default 20, entries with live
placements are never evicted). For very long sessions you can also
call `clearModelCache()` explicitly, and `engine.dispose()` (via
`ARView.destroy()`) releases everything on teardown. Prefer
`switchModel()` over repeated `placeModel()` calls for product
switching, it reuses the placement instead of adding a new model.

## `takeScreenshot` returns `CAMERA_CAPTURE_UNAVAILABLE`

The session has no WebXR camera access. Since 1.1.0,
camera access is an explicit opt-in: start the session with
`enableScreenshots: true` (`ARView.create()` or `startSession()`),
`lightEstimation: true` no longer requests it. On browsers that
don't expose camera frames at all, the code is expected even with
the opt-in. Screenshots are best-effort: branch on `result.success`
and hide the feature when it fails. See
[Screenshots](/docs/guides/screenshots).

## An awaited `hitTest` never resolves after the user exits AR

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The fallback hit-test path used to hang
if the session ended first; it now settles on every path, including
session end.

## `npx cap sync` didn't register the Android plugin

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The package now ships the `capacitor`
metadata key, and `cap sync` auto-discovers the plugin, verified
in a clean scratch Capacitor app (plugin in
`capacitor.plugins.json`, `:reticlexr` in the generated settings,
no manual `settings.gradle` edit). If discovery still fails, check
you're on 1.1.0+ and that `node_modules/reticlexr/package.json`
contains the `capacitor` key. See
[Capacitor setup](/docs/getting-started#capacitor-setup).

## Importing the package in a non-React app pulls in React

Partly by design in 1.x: the package **root** still re-exports
`useARCore` as a deprecated alias, and that entry imports React.
Framework-agnostic code should import the subpaths instead,
`reticlexr/ar-view`, `reticlexr/web`, `reticlexr/gestures` never
touch React, and the hook lives at `reticlexr/react`. The root
re-export is removed in the next major version.

## A second native `startSession` shows a session but no rendering

**Fixed in 1.1.0.** The native render loop now has
a dedicated stop flag and the plugin forwards Capacitor's
pause/resume/destroy hooks, so a session restarted after
`stopSession` in the same app run renders normally.
